title: The abduction
hook: Ravana's chariot; Jatayu the eagle dies trying

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lakshmana rekha, the line in the dust, and a holy man at the door asking for food. Hold the line.

Sita steps out to give the wandering holy man his food. An ordinary kindness: a guest at the door, a bowl of rice. And the holy man changes. The orange robe is gone, and a king stands in the clearing, ten heads, twenty arms, tall as a tree. Ravana. He tells her who he is and what he wants, and when she refuses, he takes her. He lifts her into his chariot, and the chariot rises off the ground. Sita screams for Rama, for Lakshmana. She calls to the trees, the river, the deer, asking them to tell Rama where she's gone. And one creature hears her.
screen: `A GUEST AT THE DOOR.` → `THE ROBE FALLS AWAY.` → `THE CHARIOT RISES.` → `ONE CREATURE HEARS.`

segments.voice: His name is Jatayu. Some tellings call him an eagle; Valmiki calls him a king of the vultures, very old, and a friend of Rama's father. He's asleep in a tree when he hears Sita. He wakes, sees the chariot, does the math. Ravana is young, armed, a king of demons. Jatayu is ancient, with nothing but a beak and claws. He goes anyway. First he talks: put her down, he tells Ravana; a king shouldn't do what he'd punish in others. Ravana doesn't stop. So the old bird attacks, and he's good at it. In Valmiki's telling he smashes the chariot, kills the donkeys that pull it, breaks Ravana's bow, tears at his arms. For a few minutes, the old vulture is winning. Then Ravana draws a sword and cuts off his wings. Jatayu falls. Ravana gathers Sita up and flies south, toward the sea, toward Lanka. On the way Sita does something clever. She drops her jewelry, wrapped in a piece of her cloth, onto a hilltop where some monkeys are watching. A trail. Hold onto that. Jatayu lies bleeding, and holds on long enough to tell Rama, when he comes, which way she went. Keep the score honestly. Jatayu lost. He did not save Sita. By any scoreboard, he failed. The Ramayana never treats it as failure. When the old bird dies, Rama performs his funeral rites himself, the way a son would for a father, honoring the one who tried and lost as if he'd won.
screen: `JATAYU: OLD, AND GOES ANYWAY.` · `FOR A MOMENT, HE'S WINNING.` · `THE WINGS ARE CUT.` · `HE LOST. RAMA HONORS HIM LIKE A FATHER.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who fought for you and lost: a parent who argued with a school and didn't win, a friend who stood up for you and got talked over, a teacher who tried. Maybe you never thanked them, because it didn't work. Do what Rama does and honor them anyway, not for the result but for the trying, and hold them there with some gratitude.
The abduction. Sita carried off in Ravana's flying chariot, and an old bird who throws everything he has at it.
Your line: he tried. In this story, an old bird who lost still counts. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Hindus hear the story of Sita's abduction in Ramayana readings, in the Ramlila plays staged across north India before Dussehra, and on television; Jatayu is honored for giving his life for Sita, and places in India are pointed to as where he fell.

original.note: Sanskrit: the name of the old vulture king, Jatayu, whom many tellings call an eagle.
